caption:
Tidal will start removing songs made entirely by AI on December 9.
The streaming service says 43% of the tracks sent to it in the last 90 days were fully AI-generated, and about 27 million AI tracks already sit in its catalog.
Songs made with AI help can stay. Distributors will be banned from delivering 100% AI tracks.

Should Spotify do the same?

paragraphs.text: Tidal said on November 24, 2026 that it will ban and remove songs generated entirely with AI from its streaming service. According to TechCrunch and Mix, the removals begin on December 9, and from that date the company will also reject new deliveries of wholly AI-generated music.

The company gave a blunt reason. Over the past 90 days, 43% of all tracks distributed to Tidal were detected as wholly AI-generated, Tidal said. Mix reported that the detection relies on technology from Ircam Amplify, Tidal's AI detection partner, and that on November 6 more than 60% of the deliveries Tidal received were fully AI-generated, the largest influx the company had seen.

About 27 million tracks in the catalog are currently tagged as fully AI-generated, which Tidal says is 6.3% of all the music available on the service. According to the company, 96% of those tracks have received no streams. TechCrunch reported that the process will lead to more than 29 million songs being deleted by the end of the year, and that Tidal expects to reject roughly 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day under the new rules.

Tidal will also bar distribution services from delivering tracks that are 100% AI-generated and will reject submissions whose metadata says the music was made solely with AI tools. Music that was assisted by AI, but is not purely the output of an AI tool, will still be accepted, the company said.

Mix reported that Tidal has also removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for suspected impersonation of an artist's name. In a statement, Tidal acknowledged that new songs often take time to find an audience, but argued that at the current scale, music made by real artists gets buried.
Why the earlier policy was not enough

The move goes further than the policy Tidal announced in June 2026. At that time, the company said it would place an AI badge on music it detects as wholly AI-generated, remove releases that impersonate artists, and stop paying royalties to tracks that are 100% AI-generated. Robert Anderson, who leads Tidal Music, wrote on X that tagging and demonetizing those tracks did not deter uploaders enough, according to TechCrunch.

TechCrunch noted that Bandcamp has already banned AI music outright, while Deezer supplies detection tools to other streaming services and has said it will let users filter out AI music. Spotify and YouTube Music have so far labeled AI-generated music rather than removing it.

Tidal's numbers show why labels and royalty cuts did not solve the problem: when a large share of uploads cost almost nothing to produce, even tracks that earn nothing still clog the catalog and the review pipeline. A full ban shifts the burden to detection, and the reliability of tools like Ircam Amplify's now decides which songs stay online.

The removals start on December 9. The next thing to watch is whether larger services such as Spotify and YouTube Music move from labeling to removal, and how Tidal handles artists who say their AI-assisted songs were flagged by mistake.
